speechtext: I should like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs if he would comment on the press report today that Canada has sent a note to its western allies favouring a thorough re-examination of western policy on the questions of Berlin, Germany and European security, with a view to revising the current accepted policy of German reunification through free elections?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: POSSIBLE REVISION OF POLICY ON REUNIFICATION
speechtext:
I thank the Leader of the Opposition for giving me notice of this question, Mr. Speaker. I may say I am indeed grateful to him for the question. The report in today's Globe and Mail on the Canadian attitude toward the Berlin situation is both inaccurate and misleading.
Obviously a question of such magnitude is under constant study within the NATO alliance. Hon. members will recall that at the NATO ministerial meeting last December, which I attended, there was a discussion of the Berlin situation, and at the conclusion of the meeting a statement was issued part of which reads as follows:
The demands expressed by the Soviet government have created a serious situation which must be faced with determination . . . The member state* of NATO could not approve a solution of the Berlin question which jeopardized the right of the three western powers to remain in Berlin as long as their responsibilities require it, and did not assure freedom of communication between that city and the free world. The council considers that the Berlin question can only be settled in the framework of an agreement with the U.S.S.R. on Germany as a whole. It recalls that the western powers have repeatedly declared themselves ready to examine this problem, as well as those of European security and disarmament. They are still ready to discuss a)l these problems.
It would not be useful or fitting, Mr. Speaker, if any member of the alliance were to make public the details of our current discussions. I can say, however, that the Canadian government has not yet taken any position on new proposals for Berlin or endorsed any modification of the well-defined western position on the German problem. Specifically, we have sent no note on this subject to any western capital. Canada is among those who favour a continuous and searching examination of the western position to ensure that the realities of the present situation are taken into account, and we are participating in that examination.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, January 29, consideration of the motion of Mr. W. H. Jorgenson for an address to His Excellency The Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last evening, I congratulated the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) of the present motion. I wish now to take the opportunity of congratulating the seconder (Mr. Fortin). I should also like to extend my congratulations to all four of the new members who have taken their seats in the house.
We have all heard in this debate a great deal from the opposition about the terrible economic conditions existing everywhere in Canada. We have heard that nothing but black chaos and misery exist and that there does not seem to be much hope for the future. All of this has come as somewhat of a surprise to me, because during the last few months I have visited all parts of my riding; I have been in daily contact with my constituents, and I did not see any such conditions as those which have been painted by the opposition. From what I was able to hear from other government members about these black conditions painted by the Liberals and the C.C.F. members, I cannot help but wonder whether perhaps those conditions exist only in Liberal and C.C.F. ridings.
I wish now, Mr. Speaker, to speak in a more serious vein. We all know that in many parts of Canada unsatisfactory economic conditions in fact exist, and they exist for a multiplicity of reasons. However, the economic policies of the present government have been and are continuing to be successful in remedying the recession conditions which were created partially by the policies of the former administration and partially by general worldwide economic conditions. Everyone knows that the recession we have experienced during the last two years has occurred everywhere in the world including the Soviet union.
In my own city of Woodstock, which includes an area for national employment service purposes in which there are about 45,000 persons, as of this morning those who were seeking work numbered 849, or about 5.3 per cent of the labour force of about 16,000. One year ago on this date those seeking work numbered 1,248. It is the opinion of the local national employment office that even under the most favourable economic conditions the number of those seeking work in such an area as Woodstock would never fall much below 450.


This great decrease in the number of those seeking work as compared with the number in the previous year commenced last July 18, and a steady rate of improvement has continued from last July 18 until the present day. What is particularly interesting, Mr. Speaker, about these employment figures is that Woodstock has a widely diversified group of manufacturing industries, the largest single employer being the textile industry.
Generally speaking I found those in my constituency who are engaged in farming to be not only satisfied but pleased with the present government's agricultural policy. Certain individual problems exist such as those in connection with those who are unable to obtain the increased compensation under the brucellosis control program, those who have lost animals because of rabies and those who raise broilers and turkeys, the latter having been faced lately with falling prices and rising feed costs. These particularized matters I should like to deal with on another occasion.
As I have already mentioned, during the last few months I have had the opportunity of visiting various parts of my riding and many of my constituents, and I have had a great many constructive suggestions made to me. Again, Mr. Speaker, I will deal with these suggestions on future occasions, but there are three that I should like to mention briefly at this time for consideration by the appropriate cabinet ministers.
First, it has been suggested by a number of persons that a special decoration be awarded to those veterans who took part in the Dieppe raid. This operation has such a special place in the hearts of Canadians that I do not feel I need say more on this subject.
Another suggestion is that anyone having an income of less than $4,000 whose wife or husband is totally disabled should be allowed an exemption of up to $4,000 for income tax purposes. This provision would cost the treasury little money, as there are few such cases in Canada, and it would bring great financial relief to those people who really require it.
For the benefit of the Minister of National Revenue I should like to say that I have found widespread interest and pleasure in connection with the television program called "Press Conference" on which approximately four members of the press gallery belabour a minister of the crown with questions for about half an hour. The impression created is, of course, that the gentlemen of the press concerned have obviously been lying awake nights for weeks in advance thinking up the most disagreeable questions imaginable with

which to confront the hapless member of the treasury benches. While this Roman carnival in miniature is much enjoyed by the public, a number of persons have suggested that a similar program be produced occasionally and that it might appropriately be called "The Hunter Hunted". Such a program might feature an eminent member of the press gallery such as Mr. Blair Fraser who for a similar period of time would undergo a cross-examination by well prepared questions on his views concerning Canadian affairs. Such examination would, of course, be made by four members of the treasury benches. Of course, Mr. Speaker, I doubt if this suggestion will be taken up by the C.B.C. If it were, I think the results would be extremly interesting indeed.
As I have already mentioned, Mr. Speaker, opposition members who have spoken in this debate have done nothing but offer destructive criticism of the government's policies, and in particular the government's economic policies. Having served for four years in the opposition I am quite familiar with the duties of a member of the official opposition. It was always my view, and my opinion has not changed, that the duty of the official opposition is to point out the weaknesses, if any, in the government's policies and to offer constructive suggestions as to how government policies may be improved. Pure destructive criticism, which is all we have heard to date, with no suggestions for improvement, has in my opinion no place either inside this house or outside it.
The excuse has been offered by the opposition that it is not their duty to offer any constructive suggestions, but that it is their duty only to point out alleged weaknesses in government policy. If this is the view point of the present members of the opposition may I say this. They are, of course, entitled to hold it, but I think such a viewpoint is illogical nonsense. I cannot help but think, Mr. Speaker, that the real reason the opposition have not offered any constructive suggestions is that they have none to offer, and that this weak excuse is made only to conceal a bankruptcy of thoughts and ideas.
During this debate the Liberals have criticized the government for not spending enough on public works and winter employment programs, and at the same time have said that the present spending by the government is too great, thus creating inflation. The Liberals do not seem to know whether they are coming or going; they seem to want to go both ways at the same time.
While the official opposition may be bankrupt of ideas respecting conditions in the world, distinguished economists and representatives of other governments in the
The Address-Mr. Nesbitt world have made many suggestions. Last summer I had the honour of acting as chairman of the Canadian delegation to the economic and social council of the United Nations, and the world economic situation was discussed at great length. The delegates from the 18 countries represented offered many suggestions as to how this world-wide problem could be dealt with on both a national and international basis. It was quite clear from hearing the report of the secretary-general on the world economic situation that not only was the present recession world-wide but that nearly every country, including the United States, was much more severely affected than Canada. Indeed, some countries such as Chile and Brazil have been so seriously affected that the leader of the Chilean delegation suggested that unless something were done to relieve the situation the Chilean government would not be able to afford to send representatives to the next meeting.
It is interesting also to note in this connection that in the secretary-general's report it was made clear that the Soviet union, like other countries in the world, was having a severe case of economic indigestion. 1 have always been told by my socialist friends that such a thing cannot happen in a planned economy. Despite the theories of the socialist planners, these things apparently do happen. I trust that the members of the C.C.F. group in this house will take note of this fact.
I should like now, Mr. Speaker, to bring to your attention some of the suggestions that were made at the economic and social council meeting last summer, and which were made by some of the world's leading economic experts, on how a government should attempt to deal with the internal economic problems created by the present world-wide recession. You realize of course, Mr. Speaker, that it would take many hours to go into these suggestions in detail, so I am going to mention just a few of the most important.
First of all Mr. Luns, the distinguished foreign minister of The Netherlands, urged governments to encourage co-operation among all various social groups in the country, particularly labour and management, with a view to keeping down cost inflation, that is a continuous round of price and wage increases. Our Prime Minister has repeatedly urged all groups in this country to do just this. Mr. Luns also pointed out that it is the task of governments to take the lead and expand internal demand by appropriate financial and fiscal policies. He

The Address-Mr. Nesbitt referred to government spending and expansion of credit to strengthen consumer spending. Again, Mr. Speaker, this government has done just that.
Mr. Phillips, the distinguished representative of the United States, pointed out what was being done in his country, and I quote:
The availability of credit has been eased and its cost to borrowers reduced. A series of actions has been taken to stimulate the construction of residential housing and to step up activity in such fields as urban rehabilitation. Measures have been taken to accelerate public construction in many categories, including water resources projects, hospitals and highways. Congress has been asked to authorize a speed-up in the purchase of equipment and supplies used in the normal functioning of government. Provision has been made for payment of unemployment compensation for periods longer than those currently provided for under the laws of various states.
Again, Mr. Speaker, this government has done just that, only to a greater extent. In this regard I should like to point out that Canada has felt the effects of this world recession less severely than the United States. Dr. Wahlbeck, the distinguished representative of Finland, pointed out as follows:
Expenditure on unemployment has heavily taxed our budget, too. According to the law on employment of 1956, "if unemployment exists or is imminent for seasonal or structural reasons, or because of business fluctuations or other factors . . . the state and communal authorities must take necessary steps to ensure employment." If it proves impossible to ensure employment "special relief work for the prevention of unemployment shall be provided."
During the last two years it has been necessary to arrange relief work for a considerable number of unemployed.
Again, Mr. Speaker, that is the type of thing that has been done by this government. Lastly, Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out certain things in the report of Mr. Dag Hammarsk j old, secretary general of the United Nations:
Experience during this recession has demonstrated once again the effectiveness of the built-in economic stabilizers in moderating the rate of decline of economic activity. The buoyancy of government demand for goods and services, the more rapid decline in government revenue than in national output that is a by-product of a progressive tax system, the bolstering of private income by unemployment compensation and by farm support programs-all these protective features of highly developed economies have acted powerfully to brake the rate of decline in national income and expenditure ... Up to the present the major emphasis has been placed upon monetary policy; thus monetary restrictions have been considerably relaxed and some encouragement has been given to housing. Fiscal action, on the other hand, has thus far been more limited, although some government expenditure has been significantly accelerated.
You will observe, Mr. Speaker, that the secretary general has pointed out that while it is most desirable to give aid to housing

projects and government spending on public works, very few countries have done anything significant in this respect. The record of this government, particularly in the field of housing and public works, need take second place to no other country in the world.
I should like, Mr. Speaker, for the remainder of the time available to me to turn briefly to a subject which I know is becoming of increasing importance to every member in this house. I refer to the problem of the older worker and the difficulty he or she has in obtaining employment if out of a job. In many cases he or she is not permitted to work after attaining the age of 65. I would doubt if there is a single member in this house who has not had many personal requests for assistance in this regard. I for one have had far more requests with respect to this problem than any other matter. I am sure many other members would agree.
It is quite impossible, Mr. Speaker, to even begin to properly present this problem to this house in the time at my disposal. A proper presentation of the subject would indeed take many hours, so today I shall only attempt to bring to the attention of this house the fact that the problem exists, outline in broad terms the nature of the problem, and make one or two suggestions for dealing with it. I hope the appropriate ministers concerned will take these suggestions, which are personal, into consideration.
The fact that the Canadian population is growing older, coupled with trends which result in the reduction or withdrawal from employment of important proportions of our older workers, constitutes a very grave national problem that requires the closest scrutiny, not only from all levels of government but from labour, industry and private individuals as well. In 1881 the number of Canadians over 40 comprised about 20 per cent of the population. By 1951 they had increased to about 33 per cent. When we consider this trend in relation to the fact that one of the chief difficulties facing the national employment service in matching unplaced applicants with unfilled jobs is the tendency on the part of employers to reject applicants over 40 years of age, one major aspect of this increasingly grave problem is illustrated.
Again, if I may refer briefly to the population figures in 1881, we see that there were 15 adults under 65 years of age to every 1 over 65, whereas today there are only 7 adults under 65 to every 1 over 65. By 1970 it is estimated the proportion will be over 5 to 1. When we consider the effect of the trend toward more pension plans with the compulsory retirement age now normally set at 65, another major aspect of this problem is seen.

We are thus confronted with the problem of whether or not it is economically possible to maintain a high standard of living here in Canada in the face of trends which show an increasing number of older people retired or withdrawn from the productive section of our economy. At the same time the effect of this trend is to reduce their ability to consume goods, and to place the burden of production and taxation upon a decreasing percentage of the population. This trend is not likely to change. I am not including in these remarks those older workers who through ill health or personal desire wish to withdraw from the labour force. I am dealing solely with those older workers who wish to work and who either cannot obtain employment or are forced to retire.
Apart from the economic factors involved in this matter, severe social problems are also created. When older persons cannot obtain employment or are forced to retire, many feel that society has no further use for them and they become depressed and dejected. Older persons in this group who have not developed hobbies and other interests during their lives are often left completely alone; their families grow up and their friends either move away or pass away. If such people could work their time would be occupied and they would feel they were doing something useful. Without the work which they desire there is often very little left but the feeling that they are a burden on society.
What is more, the present old age security payments do not begin until the age of 70 except in cases of severe need, and under most compulsory retirement plans in industry persons are compelled to retire at the age of 65. This type of regulation also applies in the civil service. As a result, many persons between the ages of 65 and 70 have great difficulty in making ends meet until they reach the age of 70.
What are the reasons which prevent older workers from obtaining employment? Since age as a barrier to employment varies widely from occupation to occupation and from individual to individual it is difficult to make a summary of the obstacles usually presented, but the following seem to be the most common specific obstacles as recorded during a recent survey in the United States:
1.	Cannot maintain normal production standards-slow reaction; reaction too slow for production; too slow on jobs involving speed. This accounts for 22.4 per cent of the reasons given against hiring older workers.
2.	Cannot meet company physical requirements-diminished strength, stamina, endurance, health and so on. Percentage of reasons given, 20.9.

3.	Are inflexible-set in their ways, resist change or criticism, lack versatility or acceptance of new ideas. 13.2 per cent.
4.	Pension and insurance costs. It is felt by a number of firms that pension or group insurance rates would increase. 10.1 per cent.
5.	Are too close to compulsory retirement age. They would not be eligible for pensions.
7.1	per cent.
6.	Prefer younger workers. Some employers just prefer younger people and do not wish to mix age groups. 5.2 per cent.
7.	Older people more difficult to train.
3.2	per cent.
8.	Are excessively absent from work. 3.1 per cent.
9.	Do not fit in with company's policy of promotion from within-the company's own workers cannot be moved up to better positions within the seniority policy. 2.7 per cent.
There are many other reasons given involving less than 2.5 per cent of all the reasons advanced for not employing older workers, and I will not take the time of the house in detailing them now; but I think it is interesting to note that pension and insurance costs accounted for only 10.1 per cent of the reasons given. This I think is most interesting, because in casual conversation this is normally the reason which the layman assumes prevents the hiring of older workers.
On careful examination not one of these reasons is found to be completely valid. For instance, the United States public health service points out that no differences in efficiency in the performance of "moderate" work were observed between the ages of 17 and 71. This finding is of great importance, since most work of an industrial nature falls within the classification of "moderate". Again, it might be noted that the public frequently prefer older people, particularly in sales or service jobs, because they are often more polite and have a greater understanding of what the sale or service involves. In addition it has been shown that older workers can learn new techniques just as fast and often more efficiently than younger workers.
Unfortunately there is not sufficient time available for me to deal with each of the objections in detail, though I hope to do so on another occasion. I repeat that there is not one of these alleged obstacles to the hiring of older workers which is not invalid to a considerable degree and in some cases, as I have already pointed out, completely invalid.
What should be done about this problem? I realize that the national employment service has a special counselling service to help older workers obtain employment. This is a step in the right direction, and I understand it has

The Address-Mr. Nesbitt been very helpful indeed. In addition, I believe the public is becoming increasingly aware of this problem, and the pressure of public opinion is no doubt helping older persons to find employment. I understand also that the national employment service has done a great deal to encourage industry to hire older workers. However, I do not believe these measures even begin to answer the problem. Sentiment is not enough, and some more practical inducement must be undertaken.
In some states in the United States laws have been passed making it an offence for an employer to ask the age of a prospective employee, but frankly I think this sort of remedy is plain silly. Anyone can easily estimate an employee's approximate age, and all sorts of other excuses can be invented for not giving employment.
It is my feeling that the civil service commission should carefully reconsider whether or not 65 should be the compulsory age of retirement. We are all aware that each individual ages at a different rate, and that many persons at 65 are just as keen and active as they were at 40. Oh, I know the reason given is that if people are not retired at 65 this creates discontent as it prevents or delays expected promotions. However, this argument becomes invalid if the compulsory retirement age is raised to some other figure and applied to everyone concerned. The fact that in certain particular cases a civil servant is permitted to continue working past the age of 65, usually, it is true, in a position of less authority and for less money, is of course a help, though hardly an answer to the problem.
Since the great majority of persons who have difficulty in obtaining employment because of age are industrial workers of one kind or another, I think a good partial answer to the problem would lie in extending a premium to firms and businesses through the corporation tax act in the form of a tax credit where a stated percentage of persons age 65 and over are retained, engaged or rehired for work. It has been suggested that such a tax credit might be made available to any corporation employing persons aged 65 and over in excess of 4 per cent of its normal monthly pay roll. This operation would mean that the taxpayer would deduct a specific amount from the tax assessed, or he would get "credit" for this particular amount. Such a system of tax credits operating on a sliding scale would, I believe, act as an inducement to industry to employ older workers and would also make up for any alleged losses in pension plan payments due to the hiring of older workers. Government revenues could not possibly decline when reviewed in the light of an increase in the gross national product, 

increased purchasing power and increased revenues by way of sales and income taxes.
Mr. Speaker, there may be aspects of this problem which I have not taken into consideration, but I respectfully submit this suggestion to the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Labour in particular, and I do hope they will have this proposal examined. As I have pointed out, this is a problem which has many aspects-economic, sociological, psychological and so on-and I do not think for one minute that any one remedy, or even five or six of them, would supply all the answers to these questions concerning the older workers. For this reason I respectfully suggest that consideration might be given at some time in the future to setting up a special committee of the Senate and of this house to examine all facets of this problem and recommend appropriate measures for dealing with it.

Mr. Speaker, it has been a tradition of this house for anyone taking part in this debate to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. For this among other reasons I am very happy at this time to congratulate the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and the seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, as I have done in respect of others in past sessions. The parliamentary system we have works in many unusual and strange ways, but I regard this gesture which so clearly establishes the equality of a private member with all other hon. members in the house as a fine working piece of machinery in our parliamentary system.
The speeches made by private members in this debate are extremely interesting because they reflect different views on matters of national concern, and also provide an opportunity for private members to raise matters that may be primarily of local concern while at the same time of some interest to all the country. I believe the right of hon. members to raise matters of local concern and to express grievances on matters of national or local interest is an important right and a practice that we should cherish. Before dealing with the general economic situation of the country there are two matters to which I would like to address myself. One has to do with the appointments to the national capital commission and the omission of any representation on that body from the corporations of the cities of Ottawa and Hull. The old legislation did have a statutory provision for the corporations to have representatives on the old federal district commission.
My point is that in the development of the national capital plan a great deal has been done in the last few years, since the end of the last war. It has been necessary to develop co-operation among the three levels of government, namely the federal, provincial and municipal governments, and by the very nature of things that is not always the easiest thing to do. It will be understood that exclusive jurisdiction over real estate rests in the provinces, and through them the regulation of certain matters is given to the municipal corporations. Therefore it is necessary, by the nature of the development of the national capital plan, that the municipalities be full participants in any development that takes place here.

speechtext: I will put them on the record in any event. Incidentally, the figures I am using are taken from the Bank of Canada statistical summary either for December, 1957 or December, 1958. The figure of government of Canada direct funded debt outstanding, including guaranteed funded debt, as at June, 1957, when the present government first took office, was $14,902 million. million, and for December, 1958 was $13,271 million. That is an increase of $1,772 million. In other words, these figures indicate that here is a matter that should be discussed, a matter that must cause concern because without explanation the figures tend to indicate a sharp degree of inflation possibly contributed to directly by the government's financing methods.
The other figures I want to put on the record have to do with the distribution of government of Canada direct and guaranteed securities. Taking the same dates again, the increase in government securities held by the chartered banks and Bank of Canada is $1,244 million, and the total increase is $1,509 million. I can break down the figures but perhaps that will illustrate my point. These figures show that of all this vast increase in government financing plus new funded debt issues, a very abnormal proportion has gone into the hands of the chartered banks and the Bank of Canada, thereby causing the currency to be inflated unduly, while a very small proportion has gone into the hands of the public. The Address-Mr. Mcllraith
There is something I wish to refer to in addition to what the Royal bank president said, and I recognize that the minister is not directly answerable to him; I quite appreciate that fact. The Address-Mr. Mcllraith he delivered in the Royal York hotel on January 5, 1959. I quote from the text delivered by his own office. This is what the Minister of Finance said:
X have said that the conversion operation was an overwhelming success. It has earned the outspoken admiration of the governments of other countries.
Let me add my own opinion. It also has done much to contribute to the problems today and to add to the inflationary tendencies. I want to quote from an article in a newspaper, namely the New York Herald-Tribune of the same date, January 5, 1959, in order to see whether the statement is correct with regard to the admiration of the governments of other countries. I want to take the government of one other country which might be dealing with Canadian business quite a bit because they have a good deal of trade with this country. This is by Mr. Joseph R. Slevin, national economics editor of the New York Herald-Tribune. Dealing with this matter he says:
Canada touched off a flurry of interest in advanced refunding last summer when it offered new securities in exchange for outstanding bonds. The Canadian experiment looked a good deal more successful than it proved to be. It was expensive and it gravely weakened the Bank of Canada's power to curb an inflationary expansion of credit.
Then he goes on in the whole article to develop that point, and he says:
The more that treasury debt management experts have looked at advance refunding, the less appealing the idea has become. As far as the treasury is concerned, the Canadians can have it.
There we have the two statements made on the same date in flat contradiction to each other, one purporting to explain that this program had the outspoken admiration of other countries and the other quoting the views of the government of the country with which we have the largest volume of trade and with which, by reason of being on the dollar system, we are more closely linked in these matters than we are with most others.
I should like to ask the Minister of Finance to take a little bit of the time of this house to explain what governments he was referring to, to explain his reasons for inflating the currency in the way he has done, and to deal with the whole matter in a thorough way.
I see that my time is just about gone.
I should like to develop this subject much more fully. I know it is distasteful to some hon. members, but I can honestly say that I consider this subject to be of the utmost importance and urgency. speechtext:
Now
that the air has cleared somewhat, Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Much has been said about these two deserving gentlemen, and I simply concur in all that has been said already. At this time I should like to congratulate Mr. Speaker, who as a result of his unbiased attitude has won the admiration of every hon. member in this house. In addition to conducting the business of the house in an orderly and dignified manner, he has been able also to inject a little good humour and clever wit into his remarks, thus pouring oil on the sometimes troubled waters.
It is inspiring, Mr. Speaker, to be part of this truly national government sometimes, and not too often in my opinion, referred to as the Diefenbaker team. It is a complete representation of all Canadians, regardless of their origins or geographical locations. It must be an inspiration to Canadian women, who make up at least one-half of our population, to see that there are three lady members of this government party. It has been said that the reason there are not more women in public life is that they have no wives to help them. These women have proven their ability in this house, and I consider they also add charm and dignity. The ladies, as you will notice, have been placed directly across from the opposition. This is just one more indication of our unselfish desire to share our good fortune with our less fortunate members across the way.
While referring to the opposition members,
I may say that I have appreciated making the acquaintance of many of them since coming to this house and have enjoyed their friendship. When I say that I am reminded of a little poem which says:
There is a destiny that makes us brothers,
None walks his way alone,
All that we put in the lives of others Comes back into our own.
I should like briefly, Mr. Speaker, to tell you something about the riding which I am proud to represent in this house. The historic riding of Hastings South, which contributed 

one of Canada's former prime ministers in the person of Sir Mackenzie Bowell, is located approximately 100 miles east of Toronto on the north shore of the beautiful bay of Quinte.
After listening with interest to other members of this house, I should like to refer to my constituency as an example of a well balanced economy. Hastings county has been known for many years as the hub of the cheese industry in Ontario. Belleville, where the British Empire cheese show is held each year, is the home of such famous names as Cookes and Black Diamond cheese and others, known not only across Canada but in many countries of the world as the finest Canadian Cheddar cheese. As an example, the vice president of the United States, Richard Nixon, on an informal visit to our area and Belleville in recent months, mentioned that he came to get some of Belleville's famous Cheddar cheese.
Our agriculture consists of mixed farming operations including milk production for all purposes, hog raising and canning crops. I would say at this point that the present government's stabilization program has brought a sense of security to the farmers of my riding. I am one who believes our over-all economy depends to a large extent on our farm people getting their fair share of the nation's wealth. I should like also to mention with pride our many junior farm and 4-H club members, who will be future leaders in our community and public life.
I would make worthy mention of some of our industries. In the progressive town of Trenton, known to many as the "air force town", where one of our largest R.C.A.F. stations is located, we have a variety of industries including textiles, paper products, silverware, steel fabrication, electronics and many others, and the town is rapidly growing. Along the Trent canal, north of Trenton, we have an industry and a community worthy of special mention. It exemplifies the opportunities this land of ours has to offer. I refer to the village of Batawa and the Bata shoe company of Canada. In 1939 a small group of men, headed by a young man of 25 years, Thomas J. Bata, surveyed and measured land on the river Trent above Trenton, Ontario. On a 1,500 acre site they hoped to build a new business as well as a new life in a new community. Over the last decade or so, founding a new business in Canada has become a common occurrence but a new community is not being born every day.
As a result of the dreams and efforts of the young man and his associates an entirely new community has grown up in my riding, the Bata Shoe Company of Canada Limited. Both are now as much an integrated part of

the growing and expanding life of Canada as any of the varied industrial projects which are elevating this great country into the ranks of the leading industrial powers. This plant not only manufactures shoes but also shoemaking machinery and products used in national defence. I also know, from personal observation, of the loyal, public-spirited citizens who take their place and responsibility in our community, truly an example of confidence in Canada's future.
The village of Frankford on the Trent river, Stirling, with another shoe factory, and the progressive village of Tweed in the land of the lakes area in our county, are examples of up to date and live communities of which we are proud. The historic town of Desoronto adjoins the Tyendinaga Indian reserve. I would add here that in the near future I trust we will have a necessary causeway constructed above Desoronto joining the ridings of Prince Edward and Hastings, for their mutual benefit.
There are many other industries in my riding, including a large distillery at Corby-ville. Some members may have heard of it without knowing the location. Time will not permit me to go into details of many other industries in my riding.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would draw your attention to the expanding city of Belleville, known as the "friendly city", the capital of our county. I should like to bring this to the attention of some of the hon. members opposite, particularly those in the front row, sometimes referred to as the brass of the Liberal party, who have been spreading gloom and doom of recent days. The opposition seemed to have confused their own political position with the national outlook. On January 1 of this year the city of Belleville annexed 3,600 acres to its former boundaries to make available the required space and services for new industries and new homes.
The last report from our local employment office, January 1, states that the number receiving unemployment assistance is down as compared with last year. Also, the winter program is helping. I realize fully that the unemployment of any one person wanting to work is regrettable, and I am grateful that our position is improving. I might add here that in June, 1957 there were 17 vacant stores on the main street of Belleville. I have been told that on January 1 of this year there were only five. I refer to the encouraging outlook in my own riding as an example to prove that our people have every confidence in the government and in this ever-expanding Canada of ours.
I would mention, too, that we had an active divisional point of the C.N.R. in Belleville,
The Address-Mr. J. A. Richard and of the C.P.R. in Trenton, including repair shops, which are being seriously affected by dieselization and the speeding up of train schedules. We all realize that we cannot stand in the way of progress, but I have requested and will continue to request that every possible consideration be given to the welfare of our railway employees who have made railroading a life's work.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would draw the attention of all hockey-minded Canadians to our famous Belleville McFarlands hockey team of which we are so proud. The 1958 winners of the Allan cup, Canada's highest award in hockey competition, they have been selected to represent Canada in the world hockey tournament in Prague, Czechoslovakia, this year. The Belleville Macs comprise a group of clean-cut young sportsmen typical of the best in Canadian manhood. They will not only be in Europe to capture the world hockey championship, but will also be ambassadors of good will, and are worthy of carrying Canada's colours to many countries in Europe.
Later this session I trust we will have an opportunity to discuss the financing of Canadian entries in international sports competitions. I might say it has taken a great deal of effort on the part of civic-minded citizens of Belleville, as well as Mayor McFarland of Picton, Ontario, to make this Canadian entry in the world hockey tournament possible. I know they would want me to express appreciation to all who have contributed, and I add my personal thanks to members of this house for their help and encouragement.
I am sure the best wishes of every Canadian will go with our worthy representatives of our most popular national sport, who will be leaving Canada Sunday next, February 1. I have confidence that our team will bring back the world hockey championship, and assure the noble captain and his team that we will be proud of their effort and happy to welcome them back to our Canadian shores.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

Mr. Speaker, may I associate myself with previous speakers in this debate in congratulating the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Messrs. Jorgenson and Fortin). I have no hesitation in saying that both

The Address-Mr. J. A. Richard acquitted themselves of their task with much competence and dignity. May I point out also a significant event which took place at the opening of the session. Already on a previous occasion a prime minister of Canada had introduced his son to the speaker, as a new member of the house. This year we had the honour and pleasure to see a member, accompanied by the Prime Minister, similarly introduce his daughter, newly elected member for the constituency of Grenville-Dundas. I should like to congratulate both of them and offer them my best wishes.
I must also congratulate the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet for acquainting us with the fact that the province of Quebec had suddenly become a province like other provinces. I do not believe it is good policy for a province to pout at the nine other provinces and to lag behind the others all the time. We are all Canadians and to develop normally all of us need the co-operation of our fellow citizens.
Last year, I tried to get hon. members to know more about the St. Maurice area, especially the constituency of St. Maurice-Lafleche, which I have had the honour to represent here for some years. When I spoke on the address last year, I told my hon. colleagues of the various natural beauties of my riding, but added that just now those natural beauties are unfortunately offset by unfavourable circumstances which have been growing worse ever since: I mean unemployment. I endeavoured at the time to offer constructive suggestions to the government, in the hope of improving the working conditions which had become alarming. But the conditions have worsened since, and the government, which is always looking for practical suggestions, has done absolutely nothing about those I had made. I should like, however, to pay tribute to my constituents for the way they tried to improve the situation. In fact, we have winter employment committees, which have been set up in an effort to find solutions to the serious unemployment problem. I should like also to congratulate my fellow citizens and compatriots for their devotion to the welfare of their people, but I must unfortunately add that there is still a great deal of unemployment in St. Maurice-Lafleche.
Mr. Speaker, I could tell you of cases of real hardship and misery that I have seen with my own eyes. After visiting those places, I had some assistance and food sent to those people and in this way they were able to

enjoy some measure of comfort. How is it, Mr. Speaker, that those periods of unemployment recur periodically whenever the Conservatives come back to power? Are they an ill omen? I am inclined to think so, as our good old folks at home often say.
Mr. Speaker, I remember the time when Sir Wilfrid Laurier came into power in 1896. I was then 9 years old and there was not much prosperity in our part of the country. In those days many Quebec farmers lived through the winter on a diet of buckwheat pancakes. May I say too that they were days that the younger members of this house have never known. Maybe that is why they let out brash outcries whenever reference is made to conditions as they were under a Conservative regime.
In those days, Mr. Speaker, only one boy in many families remained on the farm to help out his father; the others had to go out and find jobs across the border. As a matter of fact, older hon. members remember the time when farmers had to find jobs in the United States, to earn the price of their farm. However, soon after the Liberal party headed by Sir Wilfrid Laurier came into power, this yearly exodus kept growing less and less and finally stopped almost completely. Markets were opened and the lumber industry, and other industries in general, enabled us to keep in the country our most valuable capital, the human capital. I do not have to describe the amazing development which took place in our country subsequently; only those who refuse to recognize it will deny it.
In 1911, Sir Wilfrid Laurier was defeated by Mr. Borden, a Conservative. Everybody remembers the few years which followed that difficult period, but I will say no more on the matter. From 1921 to 1930, the Right Hon. Mackenzie King, a Liberal, took over. I need not add that an era of wonderful prosperity characterized those few years of Liberal administration. In 1930, the Hon. R. B. Bennett defeated Mr. Mackenzie King and the Liberal party, and took over from him. There followed a record economic depression, as everyone will remember; I, personally remember it particularly well for, at the time I was sitting on the city council as alderman. We spent whole days visiting people across the city, to bolster their courage. They were pathetic times indeed. At the time we had only so called "tokens" for the distribution of food and to keep up the people's courage. At that time, there was no welfare legislation to help the needy; there were no family allowances, no old age pensions, no unemployment insurance

either, no pension for the blind, etc., etc. In fact, we had really nothing but these "tokens" to help people keep body and soul together.
How is it, Mr. Speaker, that in 1935, when Mr. Mackenzie King again assumed power at the head of a Liberal government, that the business and the economy of the country took a fresh upswing after the election of a Liberal prime minister? The answer is easy: it is because he surrounded himself with wise people because there were qualified men to help him in his task. Then, our country was prosperous until 1957, when the people of Canada, believing in the statements of a man whose only goal was to assume power, put their trust in a Conservative government. For more than a year now, we have been going through one of the worst unemployment situations we have ever seen, a situation which is day by day growing worse. As an illustration of what I just said, I should mention that in December 1957 there were, in the Shawinigan area, 5,300 unemployed; and in December 1958, a little over 6,500. This shows that the situation always deteriorates under the Conservative governments. Is this the result of chance? If so, I think we have had enough examples of what Conservatives can do, for Canadians to place their trust forever in the Liberal party.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think the prosperity of a country is a matter of chance. As proof of this, one needs only look at the men who are managing the country's business at the present time. Since the Conservatives took office, their younger members have been very critical of such men as St. Laurent, Howe, Pearson, Gardiner, Chevrier, Martin and others. If my hon. friends opposite would only give the matter serious thought for just a moment, they would realize that this country was built by just such men, of which there is a lack in the present Canadian cabinet. Many of those young turks who have criticized, and still brashly criticize the Right Hon. C. D. Howe are not even fit to hold a candle to him. I felt great pride after I had read recently Mr. Wilfrid Eggleston's book entitled "Canada at Work", published in 1953. The book has a stirring dedication, and I need only quote it to give striking support to my assertion. It reads as follows:
Dedicated to the Rt. Hon. Clarence Decatur Howe, engineer and statesman. His vision saw the industrial and technical possibilities of Canada; his skill and courage and drive helped to realize them."
Similar comments could be made with respect to the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, who carried on, with a devotion equal only to
The Address-Mr. J. A. Richard his ability, the great work of Laurier and King. If the atmosphere we find in Canada today is so favourable to national unity between the various racial groups, I think it is no exaggeration to say that it is largely due to the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, who, wherever he went, never missed a single occasion to stress this matter of national unity.
I now wish to say a word, Mr. Speaker, on the offer made by the Prime Minister to the municipalities of the country, a short time before he left on his long world tour last October. I am referring to this federal offer to the municipalities, whereby the federal government offered to pay 50 per cent of the cost of labour for certain types of jobs to be carried out between the 1st of December and the end of April. The city of Shawinigan, like many other cities in my constituency, could have taken advantage of this offer had it been made early enough. There is no need to be an engineer, I think, to know that works of that type require planning and all kinds of preparation. I am convinced that a great many cities across Canada were unable to avail themselves of this offer because it was made too late. Moreover, in many parts of Canada it is very difficult to lay asphalt in the streets, and to build cement sidewalks, at the present time.
The Conservative government, after promising to settle the problem of provinces and municipalities, has done nothing, in fact, to keep its promises. If the Prime Minister had really wished to help the municipalities, he would have made low-rate interest loans available to them. Thus, he would have really helped them and he would, by the same token, have honoured a solemn promise of his. Indeed, the Conservative government has done mighty little for Canadians, if we consider the very few promises it has but partially fulfilled. The cabinet wants to manage the country's business with the help of suggestions from the opposition. The cabinet could very well put into practice the one I have just made and make it possible for municipalities to borrow money at low rates. This would be doing them a service and, at the same time contribute to remedy, to some extent, the unemployment problem facing the whole country.
I was really amused, Mr. Speaker, when I heard several ministers, and many young inexperienced members, criticize the opposition because it did not offer enough concrete suggestions to the government. I was amused,

The Address-Mr. Tasse first of all, because it is the man at the wheel who is supposed to do the driving; and I was amused also because the ministers do not seem to remember their behaviour when they were sitting on this side of the house. As far as the younger members who criticized us are concerned, their statements can only come out of sheer ignorance of what has gone on.
The management of a country's business is a serious thing. Too many politicians in this government have not yet realized the seriousness of their task. If they did less talking and a little more thinking they certainly would not have to wait around for suggestions from the opposition, to solve Canada's problems. It is certainly not the old Conservative opposition which governed this country for 22 years by means of suggestions. Liberal ministers were conscious of their duty and responsibilities and, when they were running the country, they were looking after the welfare of the country as a whole rather than the fortunes of a political party. We have already made several concrete suggestions to the government in the course of this debate. The opposition is under no obligation to do the ministers' job. Let the government tell us what it intends to do to solve its problems, and it will soon find out that we have definite ideas on adequate steps to do so. Now is the time for action. The ministers should consider placing the administration of this country on a sound basis and discarding politics. This would no doubt pave the way for a revival of the prosperity which was a permanent feature of the Liberal administration.

Mr. Speaker, it seems that, traditionally, it is expected of every new member, whatever his training, his experience or the extent of his knowledge, that he address the house soon after his election and express some of his views. It is therefore in keeping with this tradition and with the many other customs that give so much value to our system of government that I rise today to take part in this debate.
It is not without considerable tremor that I rise for the first time in this house, where the future of our country is being fashioned, conscious as I am of the heavy responsibilities that weigh upon us at this time when the world is holding in its hands the awesome possibility of self-destruction. While it is a great responsibility to have an opportunity to take part in the management of the country's affairs it is also a mark of confidence and an


honour that, personally, I owe to the people of the constituency of Quebec East.
And if you consider, Mr. Speaker, that this constituency has had as representatives in this house the only two French-Canadian prime ministers, Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent; if you consider the stature of those men; if you consider that for over 84 years this constituency has been loyal to the party of which those great Canadians were the cornerstones, and that the constituency has now changed its political allegiance; if you consider that it is the constituency which contains this choice historic site, the place where Jacques Cartier spent his first winter in Canada, you will understand why I must borrow the words that you yourself used, Mr. Speaker, at the time you were elected to the highest function of this house, and deplore my lack of competence and experience to fulfil such heavy responsibilities. But I find inspiration and hope in the example you have set and the admirable manner in which you discharge your duties. I also should like to include in those congratulatory remarks, the deputy speaker of the house, the hon. member for Longueuil (Mr. Sevigny), and the chairman of committees of the whole, the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Rea).
The constituency of Quebec East is famous for the quality of its people, for their respect of civil and religious authorities, for their loyalty, their stability, and their devotion to work. This is hardly surprising for many are the Quebec East families whose ancestors lived in Canada 200 years ago and many of them have ancestors who lived here even more than 300 years ago. Many of those families too are proud to number among their ancestors Louis Hebert, the first Canadian settler, who came to Canada in 1618; I trust you will excuse me for mentioning that my own family is among them.
You would be filled with admiration, Mr. Speaker, if you could visit each of the fifteen parishes of my constituency, particularly on Sunday, when you could witness the faith and the seriousness of the people in Quebec East. You could also realize what valuable assets to our country are these people's stability of heart and mind, their attachment to their institutions, their faith and the devotion that characterize them.
We all know that there are differences of opinions on certain matters between people of different regions of our country, but I

think that many of those differences will no longer exist when we all will have, as in Quebec East, many centuries of Canadian ancestors to admire.
The year just started, Mr. Speaker, marks the two hundredth anniversary of the battle of the Plains of Abraham, and I mention this to the house so as to emphasize-the better to appreciate the fact-the more intelligent way we go about settling our differences now.
The population of Quebec East appreciates the form of government it owes to the great British traditions; this appreciation was shown on several occasions and I will only mention as evidence the fact that a monument was erected in Quebec East in memory of the great Queen Victoria.
Because of those remarkable qualities of the population of Quebec East, I am proud to be its representative in this house and I promised to work for its progress and that of all the area of the province and of the whole country to the best of my ability, confident that the fact of being an engineer would perhaps help.
Before dealing with the subject of the debate itself, may I mention, Mr. Speaker, how touched I was, on my arrival in the capital, to see the coat of arms of my city of Quebec in the place of honour to the right of the parliament entrance hall. But I was even more pleased to note the great esteem and interest shown by my English colleagues for the French fact and culture in Canada. I must admit that never before had I encountered a greater desire of mutual understanding than among the Conservative members of the house.
(Text):
Just to make doubly sure, Mr. Speaker, that I have been well understood by my English speaking companions, may I repeat that I have never encountered before a greater desire and effort to understand the French fact and culture in Canada than among the English speaking members of the Conservative delegation to this house.

Much of the credit for this is due no doubt to the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker and to his ministers. To a large extent it accounts for his overwhelming success in the last election, but this attitude is one which also springs from a deep-seated conviction widespread in the party under his leadership. You may rest assured, Mr. Speaker, that the people in Quebec East do welcome those marks of esteem and their most ardent wish is to
The Address-Mr. Tasse achieve good understanding with all their fellow Canadians, with due regard for the rights of every individual.
The subject matter of this debate is whether we should submit to His Excellency the Governor General of Canada an address of thanks for the gracious speech he delivered at the opening of this session. My opinion is that it is proper to do so.
The program outlined in this speech is an obvious indication that His Excellency the Governor General is advised by enlightened and forward-looking ministers who are eager to see the development of each and every area of this country; in other words, the government of this country is in capable hands. As a further proof, Mr. Speaker, you can recall many events which have a particular interest for the Quebec East riding and which took place since His Excellency has been receiving the advice of his present ministers. One of the steps Quebec East appreciated the most, Mr. Speaker, was taken when the federal government bought the park where the first pioneers of this country, Jacques Cartier and his companions, spent their first winter and when it became a national historical park.
This site, one of the most revered of our history, had been awaiting official recognition for over 350 years, and it is thanks to the present Prime Minister and to his appreciation of spiritual values that this event has taken place, and that we can hope to see this most beloved spot made beautiful and worthy of its past. Our Prime Minister has left, in Quebec East, the characteristic imprint of his great personality, and we shall remember it.
In the economic field, one of the vital activities of Quebec city is its port. Until 1850, it was bustling with activity, and unequalled in the country. Things changed when progress, at a cost of hundreds of millions of dollars, prompted man to dig a channel allowing sea-going ships to reach Montreal, and to construct railways connecting the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts. Quebec was hard hit by these events, but found solace in the thought that it had, in a way, been the mother of various cities that grew up as a result of these works and which, today, have grown larger than their parent. But with a turn of the tide, which, it is hoped, will cause no envy, Quebec may recover to a certain extent. Owing to the extension of the St. Lawrence seaway to the

The Address-Mr. Tasse great lakes, and also to technical developments that now allow ships to travel in winter through the gulf of St. Lawrence and the lower section of St. Lawrence river, Quebec may, up to a point, recover its function as a terminal port which Providence had originally meant it to be and which she held until the middle of the last century. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) and the staff of his department deserve to be congratulated for the boldness and progressiveness which they have shown in the highly important field of seaway transportation, which is so particularly important for the Quebec area.
In a similar vein, Mr. Speaker, the St. Charles river, which is now a liability, may well become a great asset for our city, by the building of locks and walls. It is rather unusual to see that the works which were undertaken about 1911 as a result of an agreement between the city of Quebec and the federal government and for which close to $2 million were spent, and which were put aside because of the war, were never resumed by later administrations. But the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) was quick in realizing the importance of those facilities for the development of Quebec and he hastened, as soon as he was requested to, to order a survey of the situation to see what could be done about it. I trust, Mr. Speaker, that his able departmental engineers will find a suitable solution to the difficulties that have accumulated as a result of the discontinuation of these works, in order to give Quebec city what she should have benefited from for almost 40 years.
Another proof of the spirit of initiative and enterprise of this government, Mr. Speaker, is its recent decision to acquire the St. Charles home that has been vacant for many years in a quite valuable site, and to replace it by a building worthy of the federal government activities in the Quebec region. The constituents of Quebec East could hardly understand that the great men who represented them in the federal government for close to a century should not have considered or could not find a way of contributing to its expansion through projects of that kind. We are very grateful now to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) and to his colleagues for putting this project through. It is a great asset and contributes to the expansion of the most important business section of Quebec city.
Many other measures of the present government prove very clearly its sense of enterprise, and among the national measures which 
are most beneficial to the economy of my constituency, are the amounts of money made available to the building industry in the form of housing grants, increased grants for the elimination of level crossings and recently, the inquiry on discriminatory freight rates. But the best proof of this sense of enterprise, Mr. Speaker, which also reflects that desire for mutual understanding to which I referred a moment ago, lies right there in this fine simultaneous interpretation system. Canada has been officially bilingual for a long time now, and we have also heard much about unity and good will, but we owe credit to the present government for taking this concrete and important step through which we can understand one another more easily.
Mr. Speaker, the past is an excellent guarantee of the future and after hearing of the legislative program described in the gracious speech read by His Excellency the Governor General, there is no doubt in my mind about the value of His Excellency's ministers and about their ability to carry out the program outlined there. That is why I think it is desirable to thank His Excellency for his gracious speech and I will vote in favour of the proposal so well expressed by the hon. member for Provencher and so eloquently seconded by the hon. member for Montmagny-L'lslet.

Mr. Speaker, I believe there is a growing body of evidence that in many important instances the government talks one way and acts another. I think it is one of the cardinal principles of a democratic government that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) or responsible members of the cabinet enunciate policy and principle in the House of Commons and outside of it the people of Canada should be certain that they mean exactly what they say. One of the things I refer to is the action of the government on a proposed bill of rights.
No one over the years in parliament has been more active than has the Prime Minister himself in championing the rights of minorities and the rights of free speech and freedom of the press. He has been so greatly concerned with this whole field that he promised to bring in a bill of rights, and a tentative bill of rights was presented to the house for discussion last session. We contended there were many omissions in the bill; but nevertheless the declaration was made therein that

civil rights and civil liberties in this country were to be protected.
Are they being protected? Do the persons who operate government services of one kind and another have basic civil liberties and civil rights in this country or must they stand in fear that some member on the government side of the house and, perhaps even on the opposition side of the house-although as far as we are concerned, no one in this group-may write a letter to a cabinet minister saying that this particular person is playing an active role in politics, as a result of which he may be dismissed from his position? I think that prerogative of members of parliament, no matter how long it has been used, is unfair, unjust and undemocratic and that it should be abolished. I for one will never use that prerogative myself.

Mr. Speaker, I do not mind them at all. As reported at page 14 of Hansard, the Postmaster General said:
My action was taken in accord with long-standing practice that where a member of parliament personally certifies to the partisan political activity of a public servant, dismissal may be ordered by the minister concerned.
I think that practice is abominable. I think it should be stopped. I think that any government that professes to believe in a bill of rights should halt this action which is the very opposite of the action and the principles contained in any bill of rights. But the Prime Minister, when he commented on the matter did not, I notice, come forthwith to the defence of the Postmaster General. What was the Prime Minister's answer? His answer was, I was out of the country; it is not my responsibility. This was what we got from the Prime Minister. He said it was the responsibility of the Postmaster General. Surely, it is a very elementary fact that in a British democracy the Prime Minister is responsible for the actions of the members of his cabinet. The Prime Minister himself must bear the responsibility for this man having been persecuted because of his political beliefs.
If the Prime Minister wishes to prove to the people of this country that he believes not only in the principles of the bill of rights but that his government is prepared to follow those principles in every way, he would have this man's sub-post office returned to him or restitution made in some other form. Then the people of Canada would say, this is positive proof that the Prime Minister does not believe that people should be persecuted because of their political beliefs. The Prime Minister was able, and we agreed with it, to stand up in parliament last session and

My point at this time is that wrong doing, acts of murder and so forth in any country in the world, particularly on a wholesale scale, are things about which the Prime Minister of this country should be prepared to protest in the strongest possible terms. I believe this government has demonstrated in recent days another very undemocratic attitude. I refer to the attitude of the government in so far as the C.B.C. producers' strike in Montreal is concerned. I have read everything I could on this question, and I am convinced that the producers who are out on strike have one issue in mind mainly, and one issue only, and that is that they want their association to be recognized as their bargaining agency in dealing with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Since when has that been considered an unfair request? Since when has it been considered wrong for an organization, be they producers or any other body of workers, to say to the corporation for whom they work; this is our association; this is the association of our choice and this is the association that we wish recognized?
What have we asked the government to do? We have not asked the government to go in and settle the strike, to lay down the law and force the men back to work. We have said that the officers of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) and the Prime Minister should be available for the calling together of the parties in this dispute to see whether or not, when they are brought together, an amicable settlement can be arranged. What answer did we get from the government? I think we got three answers. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), to whom the C.B.C. reports, says that the strike is illegal. The Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) says the strike is legal, and the Minister of Labour says, I don't know. I thought there were only two sides to most questions, but apparently there are three to this one. It is legal; it is illegal; and I don't know. This is scarcely the attitude of a government that is responsible to the Canadian public.


We feel that action should be taken. The government should use its good offices to bring about an amicable settlement. There is no doubt in my own mind but that in good time the people who wish to see these facilities maintained and continued, people of good will, will see that this strike is settled. How long is it going to continue? How much ill will will be generated? How much of these services will be lost? Is the corporation management sincere? Are they adamant in saying that they are prepared to build the organization from the bottom up? I think the producers, the artists and all the other people who are involved in this strike have made a very great contribution to the culture of Canada. They have made a real contribution towards the development of French Canadian culture for the French speaking sections of Canada. They have accomplished great things over the years, and those accomplishments should not be endangered because the government refuses to bring the parties together to talk over the situation in order to bring about a settlement. I feel that in asking for a certain organization to be recognized as their collective bargaining agent these people who are on strike are very much in order and very much within their rights.
The next question to which I wish to refer concerns another matter in which the government has said to parliament, this is being done and this is being accomplished, whereas we And that as events take place there is little evidence that it has been accomplished. I refer to the whole question of United States policy and United States law as it affects the subsidiaries of United States corporations operating in Canada. We had a great deal of discussion about this matter last year. We had a long discussion concerning the loss of the sale of 1,000 automobiles to China. The Prime Minister had this matter discussed with the President of the United States when he was in Ottawa, and we thought an arrangement had been worked out. We felt that this kind of difficulty would not happen again.
I have in my hand a clipping from the Globe and Mail of July 10, 1958, which has this to say in part:
Mr. Fleming asserted Canadian independence in such matters.
"The intention", he said, in a note read to a press briefing by James Nelson, Mr. Diefenbaker's press secretary, "is that Canadian law and Canadian law alone is to prevail over persons or corporations carrying on business in Canada."
That should have been clear enough. The Prime Minister, in reporting to parliament

on July 11, 1958, at page 2142 of Hansard, had this to say:
The President expressed the view that the United States regulations should not be applied in any way to the disadvantage of the Canadian economy. If eases arose in the future where the refusal of orders by companies operating in Canada might have any effect on Canadian economic activity, the United States government would consider favourably exempting the parent company in the United States from the application of the foreign assets control regulations with respect to such orders.
It was made perfectly clear, and I want to underline this fact, that there was no question at any time that, with respect to the operations of Canadian companies, Canadian law shall govern and Canadian wishes shall be respected.

Mr. Speaker, first I would like personally to congratulate the hon. member for Pro-vencher (Mr. Jorgenson) and the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin) on their speeches on the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
