I would like to compliment, you, Mr. Speaker, on the excellent way in which you are carrying out your duties in this house, and I would also like to compliment the Deputy Speaker and the deputy chairman of committees of the whole house.
Like other hon. members, I should now like to inform the house of some of the very interesting facts about my constituency of Waterloo South, situated as it is approximately 60 miles southwest of the city of Toronto. Galt is the largest municipality in my riding and is just under 26,000 in population. Preston is slightly over 10,000 followed by Hespeler, New Hamburg, Baden, Ayr, Breslau and several other municipalities.
Waterloo county is often referred to as the banner county of Ontario and is known as a very rich agricultural area, the home of a very large number of thrifty and successful farmers. Most of them are engaged in mixed and dairy farming. There are feed cattle producers, hog producers, sheep farmers as well as several large turkey and broiler farms. The farmers in my constituency are generally speaking a very successful and happy group and cause me very little worry or concern.
Waterloo South is a very highly industrialized area, containing approximately 250 diversified industries, large and small. Therefore, you, Mr. Speaker, will readily agree that there are many problems which come to me as a result of the various plants in my riding. At this time I wish to thank the various ministers, their deputies and staffs for the courteous co-operation they have given me in handling some of those problems. I wish especially personally to thank our great leader, the Prime Minister

(Mr. Diefenbaker), for his interest in my riding and also the Minister of Finance, Public Works, Trade and Commerce and the Postmaster General.
The main source of trouble that I have experienced since coming to Ottawa has been that of the textile situation. Textiles have been very prominent in this area along the Grand river since this section of the country was first settled. The whole area has been hit very hard in recent years by the closing out of many old-time firms. Possibly, the change in dumping duties which was announced yesterday will help some of those industries to some extent.
At the present time our government is being blamed for the condition in this particular industry. This is entirely false. To a great degree this is just another of the inheritances of the present administration. For years back some of the older firms in my riding had no end of trouble. In some cases this might have been due to management; but several of the large mills have closed, the chief of which was the very large Dominion Woollens and Worsteds plant at Hespeler. This firm, I am told, manufactured about 70 per cent of all the uniform cloth required by the three branches of the services during the second world war. The plant and buildings have now been acquired by Silk-knit Limited of Toronto, who plan to reopen the mill this year and manufacture another line of textiles. But one point I would like to mention here which disturbs me very much is my understanding that all the equipment which was used for the manufacture of those defence materials is now being scrapped and sold for salvage. My personal feeling is that the government should acquire this equipment, put it in mothballs, as the saying goes, and have it available for any emergency which might arise because there is no other equipment coming into Canada which would replace those machines now slated for the junk pile.
It is my sincere hope that defence department officials will check into this at once because some of the finest materials available during world wars I and II were manufactured on these very looms and other machinery in this plant. In the event of an emergency it would seem utter foolishness to have to depend on importations of materials for war purposes or civilian use as well.
Importations of woollen cloth goods and finished garments from the United Kingdom, Italy and Germany have also had serious effect on the woollen industry in my constituency, to say nothing of the Japanese imports such as textiles, steel and iron pipe,
The Address-Mr. Anderson brass and brass fittings, plastics, toys, finished clothing, rain wear, woven gloves, and so forth.
One of the leading industrialists in my riding, Mr. Gordon Chaplin, the president of the Canadian General-Tower Company, whose father made quite a name for himself in this house, the Hon. J. D. Chaplin, who was a minister from Lincoln, in speaking in St. Catharines on Friday, January 16, had this to say when speaking on "Buy Canadian":
Buy more Canadian goods or face increased unemployment and depression of secondary industries in the country.
These were the alternatives offered in effect by Gordon Chaplin, a Galt manufacturer and a native of St. Catharines, in an address Thursday to the St. Catharines Rotary club.
While recognizing the importance of international trade to the Canadian economy, Mr. Chaplin pointed out that Canadian manufacturing industries are handicapped by high labour costs and relatively small volume, as well as by various types of protective legislation in countries to which Canada might export.
At the same time in the home market Canadian goods must compete with the American imports which can be produced at a lower unit cost because of the volume, and with Japanese and other goods which are produced by cheaper labour.
Mr. Chaplin noted that his own firm, the Canadian General-Tower Limited, which produces some 2,500 plastic items of materials new since the last war, has faced a radical change in the past 20 years. Not only has the firm had to keep up to date on its products, but it has lost its export markets which had been 36 to 40 per cent of production before the war. Loss of this market he blamed on currency restrictions, quotas and protective devices in foreign countries intended to protect their home industries. Canadian production has also been priced out of foreign markets and is in danger of being priced out of home markets-
"We simply cannot go on indefinitely," he said. "The government has recognized this in advocating a 15 per cent trade diversion to the United Kingdom. This may have merit, but why not a 15 per cent diversion to Canada?"
After the war the supreme allied powers and particularly the United States aided in the re-estabishment of the Japanese government and industry. Canada helped too by giving support to Japan's participation in the Colombo plan, Japan's accession to GATT and admission to the United Nations and subsequent election to the security council. In addition, Canada accepted Japan as a member of the most-favoured-nation category for customs and tariff purposes and in 1954 signed a special trade agreement. By 1957 Canada had sold $139 million worth of goods to Japan and imported $61J million. Of the $139 million sold by Canada to Japan, $53.6 million was for wheat, $13.8 million was for barley, $11.4 million for flax seed, $1.3 million for mustard seed and $1 million for wheat flour. This is a total of $81 million in agricultural products.
The emphasis on wheat sales has been the key to the whole question of Japanese and

The Address-Mr. Anderson Canadian trade because that was the main reason former trade minister C. D. Howe gave for the 1954 trade agreement between the two countries. Canada is selling its wheat and agricultural products, as well as wood pulp and metals, and we have a favourable trade balance of $771 million. The catch is, however, that these imports into Canada are based on Japanese values before duties and not on what they are worth in Canada.
With Japanese wages approximately one-eighth of Canadian wages and the whole Japanese economy geared to low-cost operation, it is estimated that the replacement value in Canada of these imports is from two to three times their Japanese value. On the basis of even two and a half times their Japanese value, goods imported from that country would be valued at $153.7 million.
In 1957-58 the largest imports from Japan were textiles and clothing, but also imported in very large quantities were toys, electrical products, rubber goods, plywood and veneers, all of which are manufactured in the county of Waterloo. I should mention at this time for the benefit of some hon. members some of the nationally known products of Waterloo county. Articles which are used in the home, factory or office, institutions and hospitals run from the largest of steam boilers which can be adapted for the use of nuclear power to furnaces, stoves, washers and dryers, sinks, tubs and toilets, refrigerators, deep freeze units, fine furniture, guaranteed metal furniture of all kinds for home, office, hotels, airports, woodworking machinery, saws, precision tools, electrical devices, controls, transistors, switches, felt boots, ladies', men's and children's shoes, woollen, cotton and silk textiles, business machines, factory trucks, cash registers, automobile parts such as mufflers and gas tanks, tacks and nails, taps and dies, plumbing fittings, plastic curtains, kitchenware, toys, rain wear, air conditioning systems and blowers, school furniture, desks and chairs, post office furniture, steel barns and buildings, magnesium products, hockey sticks, steel springs and all kinds of meat and cheese products.
I might mention here that only the day before yesterday I received from one of my constituents a copy of a letter which was addressed to the Department of National Revenue, and it points up a fact that I think should be mentioned, that under the heading of goods of a type or kind not manufactured in Canada I believe there are many imports coming in that should and can be made here. At this time I should like to say a few words about another matter that is very important to my constituency, namely the Waterloo-Wellington airport. I would remind the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) of his recent visit to the airport and the increasing need of adequate night lighting, radio control, extended runways and other matters. On many occasions when Malton is fogged in Waterloo-Wellington is clear. But aircraft cannot land due to the lack of proper radio communications and runway lighting. Many firms in our area have their own aircraft and others are subsidiaries of large United States companies whose planes returning from the United States or points in Canada after dark, have to land at Malton and their passengers have to travel to their destination at Galt, Guelph or Kitchener by car or train. It is my sincere hope that amounts will be included in the department's estimates to provide for these necessary installations in the coming year. This airport has wonderful possibilities and will serve a great many industries in this very busy section of Ontario which will become even busier with the advent of the seaway and the new 401 highway.

There are quite a few members of the house who have served for years on municipal councils and some like myself as mayors of their municipalities. This is a very good training for a grass roots approach to the responsibilities of a member of parliament. There is, however, a vast difference in the way a municipal government operates and the way parliament carries out its duties. I believe that a strong, active opposition is very essential and necessary but not to the degree that they should try to block or stall for political reasons all sound and sensible legislation put forward by the government. In my years of municipal experience we often had members with vastly different views but in a democratic and sensible way we settled our differences and then went on to do the job we were elected to do.
This brings up another point, that of the extraordinary co-operation we received from the civil employees and departmental heads. In all cases they were very loyal and cooperative and I personally was shown every co-operation. This is the way it should be. In private business you cannot be successful if your staff are not co-operative and loyal. From my personal observations I feel that a large percentage of the government employees are loyal and co-operative, but I am sorry to say that in my opinion there are some yet who depend on a government cheque for services rendered who do not realize that, as a result of the June 10, 1957, and March 31, 1958, elections, they now work under a Progressive Conservative government. They should and must be loyal to their employers or be replaced by someone who will be loyal. I do not believe in mass firing but I insist on loyalty. This is only a natural expectation regardless of which party is in power. This is a matter which I hope is soon cleared up.
There is a general feeling of optimism in Waterloo South, one which should be encouraged all over the country. I get weekly reports from Mr. Robert Oliver, manager of our national employment office in Galt. Applications at this particular time for benefits are down approximately one-third from the number at the same date last year.
We have several new plants opening up soon. There are opening up this year two large plants which I am told led to believe will employ from 300 to 400 employees for the balance of this year and we are optimistic about that matter. As was mentioned here in this house the other day, it is true that one of our textile firms is moving to Jamaica. I am sorry to see them leave Canada, but the company's decision has already been made. They have not yet moved but the decision has been made and we wish them every success.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Now that the Liberal party has been put by its leader and by its unanimous vote in the house the other night among the ranks of the social and economic planners, then indeed they might as well echo those famous words of the late Mitchell F. Hepburn because evidently they have swung well to the left. Social and economic planning to anybody who is not just indulging in hair-splitting and sophistry has a well understood significance. It means socialism. It means planning from the top and that, Mr. Speaker, as hon. members know, means regimentation.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, there is the C.C.F. ally of the Leader of the Opposition coming to his rescue, and how he needs rescue!
I propose to speak now about one of the problems which has been discussed in the course of this debate. We have heard a good deal about the problem of inflation and here is a place where, if the opposition had done its duty, it could have given a real service in this session. How have they read the difficult signs of the times? No one who is acquainted with the facts will deny that we have in the economy today, not just in Canada but in the economy of North America, not to mention other countries, a co-existence of forces that are certainly in conflict with one another. There are forces at work in the economy that are classed by nature as deflationary. There are others co-existing with them that can only be classed as inflationary. How does the opposition read them? It would have been of interest and assistance to know, but we shall never know.
There have been many diagnoses of this situation. But, I put one before you from an extremely competent source. These are remarks that were uttered in Cincinnati on January 17 by Mr. Lambert, general manager of the Toronto-Dominion bank. I am quoting now from the press release of Mr. Lambert's speech. I have it in my hand as hon. members will see.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Thank you.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I read from the press release as follows:
A Canadian banker has stated to a group of U.S. businessmen that traditional methods of monetary control in dealing with the current trend in rising prices is more likely to result in increased unemployment than end the price rise.
Allen T. Lambert, vice-president and general manager of the Toronto-Dominion bank speaking to the Commercial Club of Cincinnati, said that if today's rising prices were a form of inflation, it was of a nature more subtly based than anything experienced before and as such would require "equally subtle handling".
"It is not very helpful to describe the government deficit in Canada as inflationary at the present time," said Mr. Lambert, "though it is possibly not premature to talk of balancing the budget and it would certainly be a great boost to morale if we could be assured that we would see the budget not only balanced but actually put into surplus at the appropriate state of business recovery."
Tight money now, the speaker continued, would discourage business expansion without bringing any material lessening on the upward pressure on prices.
Then he proceeds to discuss various forms of restraint. It is quite clear that there is no condemnation in that view of the approach of the government to this problem. Indeed, the approach of the government has been based upon a recognition of the co-existence of these two factors in the economy, namely unemployment which is normally associated with a deflationary situation and the inflation to which I have referred.
The government takes and has taken a serious view of the inflationary forces at work in the economy. I have tried to describe them in rather strong terms at times because inflation is a thief and an extremely sly one. I have said that the government welcomes the evidence of concern on the part of the Canadian people over this danger of inflation because when the people become concerned about it the hand of parliament is strengthened in addressing itself to measures to combat it.
But, Mr. Speaker, there are two observations I mean to make. The first is that this danger is not new and the second is that what exists today is not overt inflation. Certainly any conclusion that there is overt inflation is not justified by the facts. What is existent today and what all of us in this chamber must take account of is the fear of inflation and such factors in the situation as have given rise to that fear in so far as it is a legitimate fear.
No one is going to do a service to Canada in the situation by simply playing on that fear. Surely what we require is a calm, realistic, unflinching grasp of the facts. That is the first requirement. The facts of this situation today can only be fairly appreciated and judged in the light of the trends
The Address-Hon. D. M. Fleming that have occurred in the past. When our friends opposite have been ringing the changes in this debate and, whether they intended to do so or not, have been following courses that cannot have any other effect than to increase the fear without making any constructive contribution whatever to meeting the problem, I say that they should be the last ones to accuse the government of responsibility for inflation.
Mr. Speaker, time does not permit today a review of the statistics but I cannot forebear from asking the house to consider just several of them in passing. The consumer price index is normally treated as the readiest indicator of price trends as they affect the average citizen. In 1935, when the Liberal government came into office, the adjusted consumer price index at the latest reading 60. When the Liberal government went out of office in June 1957 the consumer price index stood at 121.6. It had doubled in those years of Liberal administration. Today the consumer price index at the latest reading stands at 126.2. We do not take any joy out of the fact that in the past 19 months there has been a rise. But, Mr. Speaker, we ask those who wish to form a fair judgment as to where responsibility lies, to put those two facts side by side and to ask themselves what gave rise to the danger of inflation and where the principal responsibility lies.
We heard a great deal about the deficit. If this deficit is not going to be a billion dollars this year, it will not be for lack of effort on the part of opposition spokesmen, because these expressions have just been rippling off the ends of their tongues ever since last summer, whether in this house or outside of it. They have spoken of the "billion dollar deficit". The Leader of the Opposition has used that expression at various times, holding out the idea that this deficit might be even more than a billion dollars. He was not satisfied to deal with the facts. He was not satisfied to say that the government's best estimate was $700 million and that they would wait and see how the estimate stacks up against the facts when the report is available at the end of the fiscal year. No; he is not satisfied to do that. He goes out and he makes it a billion dollar deficit and in doing so he creates, as far as his voice can be heard, all the bad and harmful effects to Canadian credit and to the Canadian economy that would be done to it if that budget deficit were in fact a billion dollars.
I put the same judgment of irresponsibility on every member of the opposition who has talked in this same vein. The fact is that if I were estimating the budget deficit today I would not have cause to depart very far

The Address-Hon. D. M. Fleming from the estimate I gave this house on June 17 last year. I do not belittle the deficit. I do not belittle its effects. But let us stick to the facts and let us not have the kind of invention that has been practised on this estimated deficit at the hands of members of the opposition.
Mr. Speaker, they have talked about this deficit as though it were the only deficit that had ever occurred. I do not suppose anybody will take great joy out of the fact that there have been a great many more deficits than surpluses in Canadian federal history. However, I think it is a fact that we must bear in mind if we would have a fair, just and balanced understanding of the present deficit and its relationship to the economy and to Canadian history.
In the years that have passed since confederation, the 92 years for which we have the full figures, there have been deficits in 68 of those years and surpluses in just 24 of them. If we come down to the most recent times, you will remember that there were deficits in 1955 and in 1956; that there was a surplus in 1957, and that there was a small deficit in 1958.
Hon. members opposite talk as though this budget deficit had no peer in Canadian history. Again, Mr. Speaker, we make no attempt to disguise the fact that this is the largest peacetime budget deficit in Canadian history, being an estimated $700 million. But, Mr. Speaker, let us compare this deficit-and I am comparing it in terms of size-with the deficits that were necessarily incurred in world war II. They were as follows: 1943, $2,138 million; 1944, $2,557 million; 1945, $2,558 million; 1946, $2,123 million.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: There was a war on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I cite these facts not because it was improper that there should be budget deficits at that time-it was inevitable that there should be-but to restore something of a sense of balance in comparison in the interests of fair, reasoned and balanced judgment.
When we report a monthly surplus, as we did in the month of December, do we receive any credit for that from the opposition? No, we do not. The fact is that in December, on the accounts of the month, we did report a surplus, but what does the local Liberal paper say about it? Is there any mention of that fact? Oh, no, here is how the headline of January 24 in that paper reads: "Federal deficit figures growing". This headline is untrue. The deficit, as it existed on November 30, was reduced by the surplus reported in the month of December. We did not receive any credit for that, but

that does not matter. We are not asking for credit, but we are asking, on the part of hon. members opposite and from the press which is like-minded a little sense of responsibility in relation to the credit and good name of this country.
Then they talked about the surplus that was earned in the fiscal year before they went out of office. Hon. members will remember running into this Liberal question up and down the hustings, what became of the surplus that they amassed in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1957? What became of the surplus? Here is what became of the surplus. A surplus is a matter of accounting. It does not necessarily tally precisely with the cash balance on hand at the end of the year. In this particular case it is interesting to see what became of the surplus. There was, for the fiscal year 1956-57 a surplus of $258 million. This was on March 31 and the old government went out of office on June 21 following, three months later. In those three months the old government disbursed $588 million in non-budgetary transactions. These included payment at the beginning of April of $100 million to the Canada Council; redemption of Canada savings bonds to the amount of $126 million; payment on June 15 at maturity of an issue of bonds totalling $150 million, and disbursements by way of loans, advances, pension accounts and other non-budgetary transactions amounting to $212 million net. So, you see, Mr. Speaker, these outlays on nonbudgetary transactions were much more than enough to use up that surplus, indeed to do so about twice over. They were, of course, taking in other revenues at the time and making other outlays, but the fact is that that is where this surplus went at that time.
You will see, therefore, that the surplus for 1956-57 on hand at March 31, 1957 was entirely used, along with hundreds of millions of other dollars in cash, to discharge the obligations of the old government on and after April 1, 1957. The old government disbursed it all. Two payments alone by the old government absorbed the surplus in full, namely the payment to the Canada Council and the redemption on June 15 of the maturing issue of bonds. These were proper payments in the discharge of obligations created with parliamentary authority. However, the point is that the surplus from the year 1956-57 was used by the old government in the fiscal year 1957-58 before it went out of office and it drew heavily as well on other cash funds carried over into 1957-58 from 1956-57 before it went out of office.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Will the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I have not the time now, but I shall be glad to answer questions at the conclusion of my remarks if hon. members wish.
We have heard references on the part of hon. members opposite to the high cost economy. I hope no one is going to suggest that I have not done all I can to warn all sections of the Canadian people against the dangers of developing here in Canada a high cost economy. A country that is dependent to the extent that we are on export markets is the kind of country to which the danger of becoming a high cost economy is very serious indeed. I can only repeat the things that I have said before in this regard in calling upon all sections of the Canadian people, whether they are employers, employees or self-employed, and whether they are members of this house who support the government or members in the opposition, to have regard for these dangers. Let us all see that we take advantage of the opportunities given to us to warn the Canadian people against the dangers of a high cost economy.
Mention was made in the speech of the Leader of the Opposition of the money supply, and he gave the impression, as I did my best to follow him, that the holding of government bonds in the banking system as distinguished from public hands was growing. The fact is that that situation was reversed last autumn.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I think I should explain at once, Mr. Speaker, that I perhaps gave the wrong impression. My figures were for the end of September.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is unfortunate my hon. friend did not make his point much clearer than he did. It is true that there had been, up to that date, an increase in the public debt held in the hands of the banking system compared with that in the hands of the public. I am happy to say to the house that in the autumn months that trend was reversed, and happily reversed. We have had the situation since, thanks to the unprecedented success of the Canada savings bond issue last autumn, where there has been a notable reduction in the proportion of public debt held by the banking system and a relatively substantial increase in the public debt held in the hands of the public as distinguished from the banking system. I am glad the hon. gentleman has taken advantage of this opportunity to clear up what he said on that occasion because obviously the other impression was completely unjustified by the facts.
I had hoped to say something today about the conversion loan. I have time only to
The Address-Mr. Carter mention this, that we are deriving today very great and timely benefits from the tremendous success of the conversion loan last year. Do hon. members realize what kind of situation we would have faced in this month of January with the fifth victory loan maturing and over a billion dollars to meet or to refund in some way? Do hon. members realize, if we had not taken the steps we did at that time, what it would have meant to this country, with the rise in the interest rates since last summer and the softening of the bonds markets of this continent, to have to face now in addition to our current borrowings a maturity of more than a billion dollars? I think all members may well realize what benefit has accrued to Canada from the fact that we were successful, with the co-operation of the holders of over 90 per cent of these victory loan bonds, in postponing the maturity of that indebtedness. It is the sort of thing we could not do to-day. We may be thankful we accomplished it when we did.
Some hon. members opposite have been talking about the weakness of the bond markets on this continent as though it were something that gave them sheer glee. The fact is that there has been a very serious decline, and it would have hit this country much sooner than it did had it not been for the success of the conversion loan. However, the effects of the weakness in the New York bond market, the very serious weakness, could not fail to be felt in the bond markets of this country. You cannot isolate Canada from the economic influences of the United States, and you cannot isolate the Canadian bond market from the influence of the severe weaknesses of the United States market.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the minister, but I must inform him his time has expired.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I see
that I am faced with the task of compressing a 20-minute speech into seven or eight minutes and that is going to wreak havoc upon the masterpiece I have prepared for this occasion. As I listened to the minister who has just taken his seat, I could not help but recall those words of Kipling to the effect that the tumult and shouting dies, the captains and the' kings depart. Certainly there was plenty of tumult and plenty of shouting, and there was even a long peroration on inflation, but very little information on government policy.
This curious reluctance on the part of ministers opposite to take the people into their confidence and divulge what they intend to do about the twin problems of unemployment and inflation has characterized this debate

The Address-Mr. Carter throughout its entire course. Instead of telling us what their plans are, they have lectured us on the responsibility of the opposition; they have heaped personal abuse upon us and we have been called prophets of doom and gloom because we have ventured to call attention to some of the problems which concern the nation at this time. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) made these points very emphatically in the speech he has just completed, but 1 wonder if he considers the president of the Royal Bank of Canada to be a prophet of doom and gloom, because the latter calls attention to the fact that prices today are near the explosion point. I think his words were that prices were being inflated to the point of explosion danger.
If we are prophets of doom and gloom we are in very good company, because we are in the company of bank presidents, leaders of finance and all the people who are in a position to form an intelligent opinion on this subject. Jeers and personal abuse are no substitutes for sound argument, and the fact that the government has had to resort to these tactics indicates that it is on the defensive and that it has no sound policies to put forward and no effective answers to our criticism.
Speeches which have been made by ministers in the course of this debate disclose a curious idea that members of the opposition are elected to parliament in order to formulate policy, and that it is the responsibility of the government to attack the policies of the opposition. We have continually been asked for suggestions and criticized for not putting them forward. The government has been charged in the course of this debate on many occasions with being contradictory. Certainly, one of the statements which has just been made by the Minister of Finance contradicts statements made by some of his colleagues. Hon. members will recall that the minister, like his colleagues in the cabinet, criticized us for attacking the government. I wish to put on record the opinion voiced by one of the members of the present cabinet, the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer), and I intend to read from a verbatim report of a television press conference which took place on January 30, 1956.	*
Mr. Levesque of the C.B.C. put a question to the Solicitor General which reads as follows:
If today or tomorrow you were in power, what essential difference could we note? Have you any idea on the subject?
To which the Solicitor General replied:
The role of an opposition in a democracy is to criticize legislation as it is brought down by the party in power.


I say to the Minister of Finance and to his colleagues the same words which the Prime Minister himself said to the labour delegation the other day: you certainly cannot have it both ways.
Now I should like to come to the point which necessitated my intervention in this debate, but before doing so I should like to join in congratulating the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jorgenson) and the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin) on the excellent contributions they made to the debate in moving and seconding the address.
Yesterday, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) made a stirring appeal to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) to divert the motor vessel William Carson from Port aux Basques to the terminal at Argentia. I should be failing in my duty if I did not try to put on record some of the counter arguments with regard to this proposal. The first point I wish to make is that the terminal at Port aux Basques and the ferry service between North Sydney and Port aux Basques are part of the terms of union between Canada and Newfoundland. This is a solemn pact which is now part of our constitution, and though the hon. member who made this appeal yesterday may not have realized it he was, in effect, asking the minister and the government to break this solemn treaty obligation. What value could we place on our bill of rights or what prestige would the government enjoy among the nations of the world if it were even contemplated for one moment breaking a solemn compact which is incorporated in the constitution of our country?
There is a very good reason, moreover, why Port aux Basques is mentioned in the terms of union as a place for this terminal, and the reason is that Port aux Basques is the only place in Newfoundland where a daily service can be operated between the province and the mainland of Canada. Thirdly, the ferry William Carson was built especially to provide that service. She is no ordinary ship; she was built especially for this service. She has three things to do and one of them is to break the tremendous backlog of freight which has piled up every year at North Sydney on the mainland-

speechtext:
I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but it is my duty at this time to interrupt the proceedings and put to the house every question necessary to dispose of the main motion.
When I read the motion which was moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) I had some doubts as to its regularity under the rules, but as no hon. member objected to the amendment I allowed the debate

to proceed. Hon. members will note, however, that I did not attempt to restrict the debate to the subject matter of the amendment which was moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia. Since then I have given some thought to the matter and considered whether an amendment of this kind should go to a vote, and I came to the conclusion that it certainly should not go to a vote without my expressing doubts as to its propriety, so that it would not stand as a precedent.
On further reflection I have come to the conclusion that it is really not in order and that it should not be put to the house. I should, perhaps, explain briefly what are the bases of my conclusions, and I realize that I am not giving members an opportunity to speak to the point. Perhaps, if they wish to do so, they should do so before I make a ruling.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: On the amendment, I take it, not on the right to introduce it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes. It is clear on that point that it is open to any hon. member to introduce an amendment up until the moment when the final vote has to be taken at 5.30. My objection is to the character of the amendment. I will just explain my viewpoint by reminding the house we are debating the motion to thank His Excellency for the address from the throne.
The address from the throne is, broadly, a statement of the government's policy and the debate, broadly, is a debate on the policy of the government. That has been clearly established. Looking back over the amendments that have been moved over the past number of years they have been motions of want of confidence in broad terms rather than relating to a specific point such as the amendment I am discussing. This debate then is on the policy of the government generally and that has been indicated, as hon. members will And, as early as 1878 when the Honourable Mr. Alexander McKenzie, speaking on the address in that year, as quoted in Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 169 at page 142, said:
It has been thought desirable in our parliamentary practice that it is better to postpone debates upon specific subjects of discussion in the house until those matters are brought forward before us by a bill or resolution, and I am glad to know that the hon. gentleman admits that the speech has been constructed this time fairly in that respect.
He was referring to the speech from the throne. Speeches from the throne have been constructed in that way and have been challenged by amendments such as the first two which were moved this session and which were a broad challenge of the government's
Division
policy. On that point, Beauchesne in the same edition at page 143, citation 170, states:
170. (2) An amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne is a motion of "noconfidence"-
In subsection 3 of citation 170 Beauchesne states:
170. (3) Amendments to the address in reply to the speech from the throne are the means used by the opposition for the purpose of challenging government policies or actions when parliament meets again after a few months' recess.
Applying both principles to the amendment in question it does not challenge the government's policies. It suggests the advisability of the government introducing a motion to set up a special committee to carry on an investigation. There is no assertion of policy one way or the other. It simply calls upon the government to establish a committee to investigate the items mentioned in the amendment, the relevant words of the amendment being:
-to investigate the extent to which, directly and indirectly. Canadian companies are made subject to United States law and business policy and the damage this has caused to the Canadian economy through loss of export markets.
It calls simply and solely for an inquiry without challenging the government's policies. On that basis and on the basis of the quotations which have been made it seems to me that it is not the kind of amendment which should be accepted on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. In saying that I feel that the hon. member who moved the motion is not suffering any injustice if I am in error because he already has had the opportunity of moving an amendment which was debated for six days. I will therefore put the question on the main motion.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under standing order 55 provision is made that the house shall appoint committees of supply and ways and means. It is necessary to do so every session as soon as the address has been agreed to in answer to His Excellency's speech. I therefore wish to move, seconded by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming):
That this house will at its next sitting resolve itself into a committee to consider of the ways and means for raising the supply to be granted to Her Majesty.
Motion agreed to.

On Tuesday, which will be a government day, we shall commence with consideration of the supplementary estimates, then take the resolution preceding an amendment to the National Housing Act, then the resolution preceding an amendment to the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act and the one dealing with the Trans-Canada Highway Act.
